ingest.ground_truth: The unknown "Philippines Dushan jade" gem material was established to be tremolitized diopside anorthosite — a distinct rock, NOT Dushan jade. Establishment: PLM petrography, electron probe microanalysis (EMPA), FTIR, Raman microprobe (532 nm), and UV-Vis spectroscopy showed it is composed mainly of anorthite (plagioclase) with minor diopside, tremolite, uvarovite, titanite, chromite, zoisite, prehnite, thomsonite-Ca and chlorite; uvarovite/diopside/tremolite are the color-causing minerals (Cr3+, Fe2+, Fe3+ and charge transfer). The high RI (>1.78 in green parts) and hexagonal euhedral green crystals correspond to uvarovite garnet/diopside; the white vitreous basal mineral with well-developed cleavage is anorthite. The authors conclude the Philippines rock and Dushan jade (a zoisitized anorthosite) are two completely different materials and that the Philippines rock should be called "tremolitized diopside anorthosite." Source: Ye, Bai, Li & Sun, Minerals 2021, 11, 152, doi:10.3390/min11020152 (open access). Note: GIA Lab Note "Purple Anhydrite" (Spring 2023) was the first-choice case but GIA's JS-gated site could not be fetched verbatim in this environment; this MDPI open-access PDF was fully extractable. case_text condenses the verbatim observed-properties passages (Sections 2 and 3.1 + Table 1); PDF line-wrap newlines and the fl-ligature/en-dash/curly-quote artifacts were normalized to clean reading text.
ingest.case_text: In recent years, a new type of material called Philippines "Dushan jade" has appeared in the gemstone market in China. This new type of material, very similar in appearance and physical properties to Dushan jade, is causing confusion in the market and poses identification difficulties. In this study, eight representative samples covering all the color varieties were selected, including white, green, cyan-gray, white with black spots, dark green, and brown. The refractive index (RI) and specific gravity (SG) were measured by the distant vison method and the hydrostatic weighing method, respectively. The Vickers hardness was measured and converted to Mohs hardness values. The white sample (Q-1) of delicate texture and smooth surfaces consisted mainly of white basal minerals. The green samples consisted mainly of white basal minerals with green spots and green plaques. The green minerals were mostly euhedral-hypidiomorphic and the cross-section was approximately hexagonal. There are clear reflecting surfaces in the shape of "fly wings" under reflected light, indicating that the cleavage of the basal minerals is well developed. The white sample had a vitreous luster, RI 1.57, SG 2.77 and Mohs hardness 6.37; the cyan-gray sample had a greasy luster, RI 1.63 and SG 2.83; the green samples gave a white part RI of 1.57 with the green part over 1.78.

plain.answer: The "Philippines Dushan jade" is most likely an anorthite-rich rock (calcic plagioclase feldspar rock / anorthosite-type material), with the white basal mineral being anorthite (calcic plagioclase) and the green high-RI inclusions being a pyroxene (diopside/omphacite-type). It is a plagioclase-dominated rock imitating true Nanyang Dushan jade.
plain.reasoning: The diagnostic properties of the white basal mineral pin it to a feldspar of the plagioclase series: RI ~1.57, SG ~2.77, vitreous luster, Mohs ~6.4 (feldspar hardness 6-6.5), and very well-developed cleavage producing "fly-wing" reflective surfaces — feldspars are defined by two good cleavages at ~90 degrees giving exactly this stepped reflection pattern. RI 1.57 with SG 2.77 sits at the calcic end of plagioclase (bytownite-anorthite), which is significant because genuine Dushan jade from Nanyang, Henan is itself fundamentally a basic-plagioclase (anorthite/zoisite-plagioclase) rock — so a convincing imitation would naturally also be a calcic-plagioclase rock, explaining the close match in appearance and physical properties. The greasy-luster cyan-gray portion (RI 1.63, SG 2.83) is consistent with a slightly different feldspathoid/altered phase or admixture. The green crystals are euhedral-hypidiomorphic with an approximately hexagonal (actually pseudo-square/octagonal pyroxene-type) cross-section and RI over 1.78, which exceeds feldspar and points to a chain silicate — a pyroxene such as diopside/omphacite (RI ~1.66-1.76+) or possibly amphibole; the >1.78 reading indicates a relatively high-index mafic accessory. Taken together: a calcic-plagioclase (anorthite) base rock with pyroxene as the green chromophore mineral — i.e., an anorthite/anorthosite-type rock marketed as imitation Dushan jade. I deliberately reasoned from properties rather than recalling the specific paper.
plain.confidence: Moderate-to-high (~70%) that the base mineral is calcic plagioclase/anorthite; moderate (~55%) on the green phase being pyroxene specifically (could be amphibole or epidote-group).

ingest.ground_truth: The specimen MMS/VBN-02-102 (a right maxilla) was assigned to a new genus and species, Matheronodon provincialis (Rhabdodontidae, an ornithopod dinosaur), erected by Godefroit et al. (2017) in Scientific Reports. The assignment was established via systematic paleontology: a unique combination of autapomorphies cited in the formal Diagnosis — extreme enlargement of maxillary and dentary teeth (up to 5 cm mesiodistally), reduction of maxillary tooth families to 4 per generation, interalveolar septa alternately present or resorbed so a functional tooth sits in two paired alveoli, a shortened maxillary rostral process, a broad dorsal shelf along the rostral third of the maxilla, and more than 25 vertical parallel ridges on the labial side of the maxillary teeth. These distinguished it from the related rhabdodontids Rhabdodon and Zalmoxes, supporting erection of the new taxon. Held aside; not present in case_text.
ingest.case_text: Holotype. MMS/VBN-02-102, a right maxilla; housed in the collections of the Musée du Moulin seigneurial (MMS, Velaux, France). Referred material. MMS/VBN-93-34, MMS/VBN-09-149a, and MMS/VBN-09-150: maxillary teeth; MMS/VBN-12-22: maxillary tooth crown; MMS/VBN-02-11, MMS/VBN-09-43c, and MMS/VBN-12-A002: dentary teeth. Horizon and locality. ‘Begudian’ (local stage) sandstones, late Campanian, Late Cretaceous. Velaux-La Bastide Neuve, Aix-en-Provence Basin, Bouches-du-Rhône, southern France. MMS/VBN-02-102 is a particularly robust right maxilla (rostrocaudal length of 22 cm and maximal height of 10 cm). The rostral process is particularly short and oriented craniodorsally. The rostral border of MMS/VBN-02-102 is not eroded, so preservation cannot explain the shortening of its rostral process. In dorsal view, the rostral third of the maxilla is medially broadened to form a triangular and concave rostrodorsal shelf that likely supported the caudolateral (maxillary) process of the premaxilla. Ventrally, the tooth row is relatively straight and composed of only eight alveoli, despite of the large size of this specimen. The interalveolar septa are alternately present or nearly completely resorbed, so the base of the maxillary dental battery in fact contains four tooth positions, each of which is composed of two partially fused alveoli.

grounded_findings.finding: PRIOR: base rate of Matheronodon provincialis among rhabdodontid ornithopod maxillae from the Late Cretaceous Ibero-Armorican / southern France domain. No published quantitative base rate exists. Matheronodon is monospecific and, for maxillary material, is essentially the single holotype maxilla (MMS/VBN-02-102) from one locality (Velaux), whereas the same Ibero-Armorican domain yields comparatively abundant Rhabdodon (R. priscus, R. septimanicus) maxillary material. A reasoned (non-measured) prior of roughly 0.1 reflects that Matheronodon is the rarer of the regional rhabdodontid taxa. Graded direction_only: the literature supports the direction (Matheronodon rare, Rhabdodon common) but supplies no counted frequency.

grounded_findings.finding: locality(velaux_la_bastide_neuve, aix_en_provence_basin, southern_france): Velaux-La Bastide Neuve is the type locality of Matheronodon and lies in the Ibero-Armorican domain of southern France. Zalmoxes is endemic to the Hateg Basin of Romania (East-European / Transylvanian domain) and is geographically excluded from this site; thus the locality strongly favors a regional rhabdodontid (Matheronodon or Rhabdodon) over Zalmoxes. Locality alone does NOT discriminate Matheronodon from co-occurring Rhabdodon, so its LR for the species M. provincialis specifically is only mildly favorable. Graded grounded for the geographic root datum; the LR magnitude (~2) is a reasoned estimate of its discriminating weight at species level.

plain.answer: An abelisaurid theropod dinosaur — most likely a member of Abelisauridae (Majungasaurinae). Given the locality (Velaux-La Bastide Neuve, late Campanian of the Aix-en-Provence Basin, southern France) and the diagnostic features, this is almost certainly *Arcovenator escotae*.
plain.reasoning:
Several features point strongly to a theropod, and specifically to an abelisaurid:

1. **Maxilla as holotype with maxillary/dentary teeth referred material** — a carnivorous archosaur. The robust, tall maxilla (22 cm long, 10 cm high) is typical of a large-bodied predator.

2. **Short rostral process oriented craniodorsally** — this is a classic abelisaurid maxillary feature. Abelisaurids have characteristically short, deep, "boxy" snouts with a reduced/short rostral process of the maxilla, distinguishing them from the longer-snouted tetanurans.

3. **Only eight alveoli despite large size** — a reduced tooth count is characteristic of abelisaurids (which have low alveolar counts relative to size), again reflecting the short, tall snout.

4. **Alternating resorbed interalveolar septa / partially fused double alveoli** — this paired-alveolus condition is a known abelisaurid trait reported in majungasaurines.

5. **Locality and age** — Velaux-La Bastide Neuve, late Campanian, Bouches-du-Rhône, southern France. This is precisely the type locality and horizon of *Arcovenator escotae*, an abelisaurid named from this site in 2014 (Tortosa et al.), described from a maxilla (MMS/VBN specimens) and referred teeth. The "MMS/VBN" specimen numbering (Musée du Moulin seigneurial, Velaux) matches.

The combination of European Campanian abelisaurid affinities (linking to Indo-Madagascan majungasaurines via a Gondwana–Europe dispersal route) plus the exact museum acronym and locality makes *Arcovenator escotae* the clear identification.

ingest.case_text: In June 1979, police hunting the Yorkshire Ripper received an audio cassette tape, posted to detective George Oldfield, from a man claiming to be the killer. The recording opened with the words 'I'm Jack. I see you are still having no luck catching me.' The voice was male and spoke with a pronounced regional English accent. The Yorkshire Ripper's attacks had all taken place in West Yorkshire, in and around Leeds and Bradford. Police asked two dialect specialists, Stanley Ellis and Jack Windsor Lewis, to examine the recording and determine where the speaker came from. Ellis was a fieldworker for the Survey of English Dialects and had hundreds of comparison recordings of speakers from across northern England. He analysed the speaker's vowel sounds. The vowel the speaker used in the word 'I' was a wide gliding diphthong, a 'banana vowel', rather than the flatter monophthong heard in Tyneside or in North Yorkshire. He examined the quality of the vowels in words such as 'house', 'down' and 'about', and the pronunciation of the word 'strike', which he judged inconsistent with a Tyneside Geordie origin. The accent was clearly not that of the Leeds or Bradford districts where the murders had occurred, nor that of Newcastle. Ellis compared the voice against survey recordings he had made of speakers in the Wearside region, including the dialect of the nearby town of Washington. Windsor Lewis, an academic phonetician, independently judged the voice to be genuine regional speech and extremely unlikely to be a faked or disguised accent.

ingest.ground_truth: Confirmed answer: The speaker on the hoax tape was from the Wearside region, specifically the Castletown and Southwick area of Sunderland; the Wearside Jack tape was a hoax, not the real Yorkshire Ripper. Dialectologist Stanley Ellis, working with phonetician Jack Windsor Lewis in June 1979, identified the accent as Wearside, not Tyneside Geordie and not North Yorkshire near the crimes, pinpointing it to the Castletown and Southwick area of Sunderland by comparing the speech to dialect survey recordings, including a recording made while studying the dialect of nearby Washington. Ellis also concluded the tape was therefore a hoax, since the real Ripper attacks were in West Yorkshire about 78 miles away. How established: Confirmed in 2005 and 2006 when John Samuel Humble was arrested in October 2005 after a cold-case DNA review matched saliva on the hoax letters to his profile in the national DNA database; he pleaded guilty in March 2006 at Leeds Crown Court to four counts of perverting the course of justice. Humble had lived his whole life on the Ford Estate in Sunderland, exactly the Wearside area Ellis had identified, vindicating the dialectological attribution.

In short: the voice was a Wearside (Sunderland) accent.

Several signals in the prompt point unambiguously toward a Wearside/Sunderland conclusion:

1. The phonetic evidence given is explicitly designed to EXCLUDE the rival candidates and isolate Wearside. The "banana vowel" wide gliding diphthong in 'I' rules out the flatter monophthongal realizations of Tyneside (Geordie) and North Yorkshire. The vowels in 'house/down/about' (the MOUTH set) and the pronunciation of 'strike' are stated to be inconsistent with Tyneside Geordie. The accent is explicitly stated NOT to be Leeds/Bradford (where the actual murders occurred) and NOT Newcastle.

2. Ellis is described as comparing the voice specifically against his Survey of English Dialects recordings of the Wearside region, "including the dialect of the nearby town of Washington." Washington lies in the historic County Durham / Sunderland (Wearside) area. This is the comparison set he found a match in — a strong tell that Wearside is the answer.

Phonetically, the distinction between Tyneside (Newcastle/Geordie) and Wearside (Sunderland/"Mackem") is exactly the kind of fine-grained northeastern contrast a Survey of English Dialects fieldworker would adjudicate: the MOUTH vowel, the PRICE vowel quality, and lexical items behave differently across the Tyne/Wear divide.

4. Historically this is the well-documented "Wearside Jack" hoax. Ellis publicly placed the speaker in the Sunderland area and famously narrowed it to a small district (Castletown/Southwick), within a couple of miles. The hoaxer, later identified (in 2005 via DNA) as John Humble, was indeed from the Ford Estate/Sunderland area of Wearside. So the contemporary expert judgment was correct as to region.

Because the prompt foregrounds Washington and the Wearside survey recordings and systematically eliminates every alternative (Tyneside, Newcastle, North Yorkshire, Leeds, Bradford), the intended answer is the Wearside/Sunderland area of County Durham, with Ellis's celebrated narrowing to the Castletown/Southwick neighborhood of Sunderland.
